Hanoi (VNA) - Prime Minister Le Minh Hung on October 3 called on ministries, sectors and localities to more effectively tap available growth potential, remove bottlenecks and maximise growth drivers in the final months of 2026, with the aim of achieving the year’s socio-economic development targets and creating momentum for 2027. 
The PM made the request while chairing the September regular Government meeting and an online conference between the Government and localities, held in person at the Government headquarters and connected via videoconference with ministries, sectors and 34 provinces and cities nationwide. 
As the final months of 2026 will be decisive to achieving the year's socio-economic development targets, he asked ministers, heads of sectors, Party committee secretaries, and chairpersons of provincial-level People's Committees to continue closely following and more resolutely and effectively implementing programmes and action plans to achieve the 2026 targets, creating momentum for a breakthrough in 2027 with a spirit of acceleration, decisive action and clear results. 
He noted that to achieve double-digit growth, GDP growth in the fourth quarter must exceed 12.5%, putting enormous pressure on ministries, sectors and localities and requiring the highest level of determination and effort 
Regarding common tasks for ministries, sectors and localities, the PM requested continued improvements to institutions and laws, with the highest quality ensured for draft laws submitted to the National Assembly and all guiding regulations issued fully and on schedule. 
Efforts should be made to disburse 100% of the public investment plan, complete key projects according to the 2026 schedule and remove obstacles to long-delayed projects, he said, asking localities to actively propose groups of tasks and solutions to develop special economic zones in line with the Law on Urban Development. 
The Government leader stressed the need to strongly develop the domestic market, stimulate demand and effectively tap the year-end consumption and tourism seasons while controlling and stabilising prices; boost exports and reduce the trade deficit; promote new growth drivers; encourage private investment and attract foreign investment; and require corporations and groups to complete their investment, production and business plans. 
He called for strict price controls and efforts to achieve the 2026 inflation target approved by the National Assembly, ensuring adequate supplies of essential goods such as fuel, electricity, food, construction materials and medicines. Inspections should be strengthened and strict action taken against hoarding, speculation and smuggling. 
At the same time, the PM called for stronger development of science and technology, innovation and digital transformation, along with effective disbursement of allocated funds; completion of the “100-day campaign” to address bottlenecks in digital transformation; and implementation of tasks to develop strategic technology products based on the strengths of different sectors and localities. 
He also stressed the importance of cultural and social development and improving people's living standards; developing social housing and rental housing; resolutely implementing the 500-day-and-night campaign to accelerate the search for, collection and identification of the remains of fallen soldiers; carrying out key tasks in education, healthcare and social welfare; and strengthening national defence, security, social order and safety, as well as cybersecurity. 
For provincial-level People's Committees, the PM instructed them to closely monitor developments in their localities; urgently review and update growth scenarios after nine months; conduct specific assessments of each sector, field and target; clearly identify any shortfalls against the set scenarios; and, on that basis, adopt appropriate tasks and solutions for the fourth quarter, striving to achieve the highest possible 2026 growth target. 
They must also comprehensively review and identify all remaining growth drivers and potential reserves that can be tapped, particularly sectors, fields and projects capable of generating added value. Bottlenecks and difficulties hindering growth, especially those related to investment, land, site clearance and project implementation procedures, must be clearly identified and resolutely addressed, with issues beyond their authority promptly reported to competent agencies. 
Major economic centres and growth poles such as Ho Chi Minh City, Hanoi, Hai Phong, Quang Ninh, Dong Nai and Bac Ninh must set higher targets and more fully tap their growth potential through measures that can be implemented immediately, while strengthening their leading and spillover roles and making greater contributions to national growth. 
For localities whose growth remains below the set targets, particularly those projected to fall short of their full-year targets, the PM requested thorough assessments of available growth potential and the immediate implementation of strong, decisive, specific and effective measures to achieve the highest possible results. 
For ministries and sectors, he asked the Ministry of Finance to continue closely monitoring domestic and international developments, regularly tracking, analysing, assessing and updating growth scenarios, and promptly advising the Government and the PM on difficulties and obstacles, particularly factors affecting growth. The ministry should propose appropriate, effective and feasible tasks and solutions to boost production and business activities and mobilise and effectively use resources for development. It was also asked to urgently submit to the Government a decree providing a 30% reduction in corporate income tax for enterprises and business households with annual revenue of no more than 10 billion VND (384,830 USD), and focus on simplifying tax administration and procedures related to public investment. 
He asked the State Bank of Vietnam to focus on monetary policy management and ensure liquidity for the economy; implement measures to stabilise interest rates and the foreign exchange market; closely monitor monthly developments in the balance of international payments and proactively forecast, update and develop scenarios for timely and appropriate policy management. It should also strengthen inspection, supervision and control of credit institutions to promptly address violations, while proactively proposing solutions to expand credit and interest-rate mechanisms for social housing, rental housing, major and key projects and priority sectors. 
Meanwhile, the Ministry of Industry and Trade was urged to prepare a plan to implement the Reciprocal Trade Agreement immediately after its signing; focus on measures to boost exports, control the trade deficit and develop balanced and sustainable trade; support businesses in responding to international trade fluctuations; make effective use of next-generation free trade agreements; step up trade promotion, diversify export markets and stimulate domestic demand. 
The ministry, together with businesses, must ensure adequate supplies of fuel and electricity; soon submit and implement the revised Power Development Plan VIII; restructure Vietnam Electricity (EVN); urgently finalise and submit the decree on fuel trading; and increase coal and oil and gas production. 
The Ministry of Construction was tasked with ensuring progress on key transport projects; coordinating with the Ministry of Industry and Trade to manage supplies of construction materials for important and nationally significant projects; and accelerating social and rental housing projects. 
The Ministry of Agriculture and Environment must continue measures to improve the quality of agricultural products and meet the plant quarantine, food safety and traceability requirements of import markets; and work to have the European Commission’s “yellow card” warning on illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing lifted. 
The PM instructed the Ministry of Justice to closely coordinate with ministries, Government agencies and National Assembly bodies to finalise draft laws and resolutions for submission to the National Assembly. It should focus on appraising regulations guiding the implementation of laws after their adoption to ensure progress and quality. 
The Ministry of Science and Technology was tasked with leading and guiding the implementation of the National Digital Architecture Framework and the digital architecture frameworks of agencies and organisations; reviewing and removing bottlenecks in the commercialisation of research results; proposing improvements to regulations on science and technology exchanges; and coordinating with the Ministry of Finance to address financial and disbursement bottlenecks related to science and technology, innovation and digital transformation. 
The Ministry of Education and Training was asked to lead the completion of a programme and develop a specific roadmap for completing a new set of textbooks for unified nationwide use and providing free textbooks from the 2028-2029 academic year. It should reform the compilation, publication, distribution and supply of textbooks; coordinate with ministries, sectors and localities to complete and ensure the effective operation of existing inter-level boarding schools while continuing to build such schools in disadvantaged communes; work with localities to ensure adequate teaching staff; and review planning, budget allocations and land funds for new schools to ensure sufficient classrooms and schools. 
The Ministry of Health was requested to proactively coordinate with relevant agencies and National Assembly bodies to revise and finalise the draft law amending and supplementing several laws in the healthcare sector. It should continue efforts to ensure that by the end of 2026, all people receive regular health check-ups or free screening and have electronic health records.

On October 2, 2026, in Cape Town, Republic of South Africa, the Forum on Prospects for Economic, Trade, and Investment Cooperation between Vietnam and South Africa took place with the participation of leaders of the Vietnamese National Assembly, representatives of the Ministry of Industry and Trade, the Vietnamese Embassy in South Africa, the Western Cape Tourism, Trade and Investment Promotion Agency (WESGRO), relevant agencies, and the business communities of both countries.
The forum was one of the activities within the framework of the official visit of the high-level delegation of the Vietnamese National Assembly to Cape Town, the legislative capital of South Africa. Delegates focused on exchanging views on the business environment, trade and investment opportunities, relevant policies and regulations, and areas with significant potential for cooperation.
Integrating Strategic Partnerships into the Economy
In his opening remarks at the Forum, Vice Chairman of the National Assembly Nguyen Hong Dien emphasized that over the past 30 years, the friendship and cooperation between Vietnam and South Africa have developed in a substantive and effective manner. The upgrading of relations to a Strategic Partnership in November 2025 opens a new framework for cooperation with a long-term vision and higher demands for quality and effectiveness. Economic, trade, and investment cooperation is one of the important pillars of this framework.
According to the Vice Chairman of the National Assembly, bilateral trade turnover is projected to reach approximately US$1.3 billion in 2025; and over US$1.7 billion in the first seven months of 2026, a 45% increase compared to the same period last year. South Africa is currently Vietnam's second largest trading partner and its largest export market in Africa; while Vietnam is South Africa's fifth largest trading partner in the ASEAN region.
However, these results are still considered to be below the potential and strengths of the two economies, as well as the framework of the Strategic Partnership.
Structurally, the two economies have complementary advantages. South Africa has strengths in resources, industry, services, finance, and its gateway location to the African market. Vietnam has strengths in manufacturing, processing, agriculture , technology, electronics, telecommunications, international trade, and experience in participating in value chains.
Based on that foundation, the two sides can expand cooperation in high value-added areas such as processing and manufacturing industries, digital transformation , artificial intelligence, green economy, renewable energy, mining and mineral processing, high-tech agriculture, and supporting industries.
One of the issues emphasized by Deputy Speaker of the National Assembly Nguyen Hong Dien is building a favorable legal environment to transform cooperation potential into concrete projects and capital flows. Accordingly, businesses need an investment, production, and business environment with clear, transparent, stable, and predictable regulations; simplified procedures; reduced compliance costs; and guaranteed protection of their legitimate rights and interests.
Trade promotion paves the way for businesses.
From a trade promotion perspective, Mr. Vu Ba Phu, Director of the Trade Promotion Department, Ministry of Industry and Trade , introduced the developments in the Vietnamese economy as well as the opportunities that the Vietnamese market can offer to South African businesses.
Mr. Vu Ba Phu, Director of the Trade Promotion Department, delivered a speech at the forum.
According to Mr. Vu Ba Phu, in the last five years, the level of integration of the Vietnamese economy into international trade and investment has become increasingly deep and broad. The scale of goods trade increased from approximately US$668.5 billion in 2021 to approximately US$930 billion in 2025. Registered FDI capital in 2025 is expected to reach approximately US$38.42 billion, and implemented capital is projected to reach US$27.62 billion.
These results demonstrate Vietnam's increasing role as a manufacturing and export hub in the region. This also provides a basis for Vietnam and South Africa to explore complementary cooperation models, ranging from raw material and input product supply, deep processing cooperation, and the development of supporting industries to expanding markets for each country's strong products.
The Trade Promotion Agency is ready to act as a bridge, supporting businesses in both countries to explore markets, find partners, and implement specific cooperation opportunities.
International trade promotion programs and events such as Vietnam Expo, Vietnam Foodexpo, VIATT, Vietnam Global International Fair, along with business networking and exchange programs, are presented as channels for South African businesses to gain deeper access to the Vietnamese market.
According to Mr. Vu Ba Phu, Vietnam hopes that South African trade promotion agencies, associations, and businesses will participate more deeply in programs in Vietnam, from exhibitions and B2B trade to finding suppliers and investment partners, and building long-term cooperative relationships.
Conversely, WESGRO states that South Africa is Africa's most industrialized and diversified economy, with a size of $363 billion, a market of 63 million people, and preferential access to African markets through the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA).
The Western Cape province, in particular, has been identified as having potential for cooperation with Vietnamese businesses in the fields of renewable energy, green hydrogen, electric vehicles, battery manufacturing, high-tech agriculture, agricultural product processing, logistics, and information technology services. WESGRO has also built the Cape Trade Portal, connecting more than 2,100 exporters in the region with buyers worldwide.
Energy and business connectivity
One notable topic at the Forum was the prospect of cooperation in the energy sector, including coal trade between Vietnam and South Africa.
Mr. Trinh Duc Duy, Deputy Director of the Department of Energy and Petroleum, Ministry of Industry and Trade, stated that in the orientation of ensuring energy security, serving socio-economic development and implementing energy transition, Vietnam highly appreciates the role of international cooperation in the energy sector.
According to discussions at the Forum, Vietnam's coal import needs remain significant in the coming period, while South Africa has strengths in coal mining and export, and possesses a large-scale infrastructure system to support exports. Both sides could explore expanding cooperation by diversifying supply sources, strengthening business connections, exchanging market information, and gradually exploring the possibility of investment cooperation.
Representatives from the Ministry of Industry and Trade requested that South Africa facilitate direct contact between Vietnamese businesses and reputable coal suppliers, support access to market information, and conduct surveys and research on investment opportunities in coal mining, processing, and supply in South Africa. This is identified as a complementary area of cooperation, consistent with the requirements for ensuring energy security and diversifying the supply chain.
In addition to policy dialogue, the Forum allocated time for businesses from both countries to exchange information on needs, cooperation opportunities, and practical issues in accessing the market.
Q&A session with businesses
The Q&A session with businesses facilitates the transformation of information exchanged at the Forum into concrete connections, ranging from finding partners, suppliers, and customers to researching investment opportunities.
The upgrading of Vietnam-South Africa relations to a Strategic Partnership creates a further foundation for the two countries to expand cooperation in many areas. In particular, economics, trade, and investment continue to be important areas, with increasingly active participation from the business community.

articles.summary: Vietnam GDP grows 9.01% in nine months  Theinvestor
articles.full_text:
Vietnam's economy grew 9.95% in the third quarter from a year earlier, bringing nine-month growth to 9.01%, the National Statistics Office (NSO) reported on Saturday.
Q3 growth accelerated, up from 8.15% in Q1 and 8.81% in Q2. In the first nine months of 2025, the economy expanded 7.85% year-on-year.
Industry-construction and services continued to account for the largest shares of the economy. In the nine-month period, industry and construction grew 11.21% from a year earlier, while services expanded 8.69%.
The two sectors made the largest contributions to economic value added, accounting for 45% and 49.6%, respectively.
The industrial sector maintained solid growth as growth drivers broadened, several large-scale projects began operations, export orders recovered, and public investment accelerated. The sector's value added rose about 11.02% from a year earlier.
Value added in the services sector rose 8.69% year-on-year, led by trade, transport, tourism and consumer-related services. Domestic demand for goods, services and tourism remained high, making an important contribution to overall economic growth.
Agriculture, forestry and fisheries posted value-added growth of about 4.02%. Productivity and output of rice, fruit, livestock and fisheries increased, meeting domestic and export demand.
Investment remains key economic driver
Total realized investment across the economy at current prices reached about VND3,110 trillion ($119.68 billion), up 15.1% from a year earlier. The non-state sector accounted for 53% of total investment.
Realized investment from the state budget reached VND661.8 trillion ($25.47 billion), up 19% and equivalent to 59.9% of the year's plan, higher than in the same period last year.
Total registered FDI, including new registrations, adjustments and capital contributions or share purchases, reached $50.36 billion, up 76.4%.
Disbursed FDI hit $21.07 billion, up 12.1% and the highest level for the first nine months of any year in the past five years. Manufacturing and processing accounted for more than 82% of disbursed FDI.
Merchandise trade balance posts $19.42 billion deficit
Foreign trade grew strongly, with imports rising faster than exports. Total merchandise trade exceeded $888 billion in the first nine months, up 30.4%. Exports reached $434.3 billion, up 24.5%, while imports rose 36.7% to $453.72 billion.
The merchandise trade balance recorded a deficit of $19.42 billion, compared with a surplus of $16.87 billion in the same period last year. In September alone, the trade balance returned to a surplus of $1.27 billion.
More than 223,900 businesses were newly established or resumed operations in the first nine months, down 3.2% from a year earlier.
Meanwhile, nearly 89,800 businesses temporarily suspended operations, 33,500 were awaiting dissolution procedures and more than 48,700 completed dissolution. The number completing dissolution rose 118.8%.
Quang Ninh, Ha Tinh, Hai Phong lead in GRDP growth
Twelve of Vietnam's 34 provinces and centrally administered cities recorded gross regional domestic product (GRDP) growth of more than 10% in the first nine months from a year earlier.
Quang Ninh led with growth of 12.54%, followed by Ha Tinh at 12.36%, Hai Phong at 12.08% and Bac Ninh at 11.81%. Ninh Binh, Thai Nguyen, Hung Yen and Khanh Hoa also posted growth of more than 11%. The remaining four localities with double-digit growth were Danang, Tay Ninh, Phu Tho and Dong Nai.
Overall, the strongest growth was concentrated in localities with established industrial bases and large-scale manufacturing and processing operations. Investment, exports and services also supported economic growth in these areas, contributing to nationwide expansion.
Some localities recorded lower growth, including Son La at 5.59%, Vinh Long at 7.32%, Ca Mau at 7.37% and Dong Thap at 7.44%. A decline in electricity generation and slower growth in agriculture, which accounts for a relatively large share of their economic structures, weighed on their results.
Average consumer prices rose 4.52% in the nine months from a year earlier. Core inflation increased 4.26%.
Whole-year GDP prospects
Nguyen Thi Huong, head of the NSO, said Q3 growth was "very high compared with many years, providing an important foundation for the full year".
"However, achieving double-digit growth remains a major challenge in the final three months, as the highly open economy remains exposed to fluctuations in trade, energy supplies and international transport costs," she told a press meeting.
For the final months of the year, the NSO recommended continuing to promote growth while maintaining macroeconomic stability and controlling inflation. Key priorities include accelerating public investment disbursement, removing obstacles to support production, helping domestic businesses improve their export capacity and stimulating consumer demand.
The agency also said authorities should closely monitor the conflict in the Middle East, oil prices, transport costs and exchange rates so that growth and inflation scenarios can be updated in a timely manner.
On April 24, the National Assembly, Vietnam's legislature, set a 2026-2030 agenda targeting at least 10% average annual GDP growth.
The Asian Development Bank (ADB) on September 23 raised its forecast for Vietnam’s economic growth in 2026 to 7.8% from 7.2% in July, the highest in ASEAN, but warned that rapid investment and credit growth could amplify financial vulnerabilities and narrow policy space.
Singaporean bank UOB late on September 18 revised up its 2026 GDP growth projection for the country to 8.5%, projecting that growth momentum would continue to be driven by improving domestic demand, investment inflows into the manufacturing and technology sectors, and large-scale infrastructure projects currently underway across the country.
The S&P Global Vietnam Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) dropped to 51.9 in September from August's reading of 53.3, thereby signalling a smaller improvement in the health of the sector at the end of the third quarter.
While the manufacturing sector remained in growth territory in September, data showed that the international environment limited the pace of expansion. New export orders were down, the war in the Middle East caused further rises in the cost of fuel and oil, and international shipping delays contributed to longer supplier delivery times, S&P Global Market Intelligence stated.
Vietnam's economy grew 8.02% in 2025, its second-fastest pace in the past 15 years, driven mainly by services and industrial production.

Money withdrawn from gold, stocks, and real estate is returning to banks.
Speaking to Tuoi Tre newspaper , Mr. Quan Vu - Deputy Head of Securities Research Department at Vietcap - said that the high increase in deposit interest rates over the past year is one of the main reasons for the outflow of money from investment channels such as stocks, real estate, and gold, and its return to banks.
The latest figures from the State Bank of Vietnam reflect this trend, with household deposits increasing sharply by 8.6% in the first seven months of the year, compared to only a 1% increase in deposits from economic organizations.
"Based on Vietcap's recent discussions with several banks, this trend is expected to continue in the third quarter," Mr. Quan said.
Vietcap experts also pointed out that liquidity on the three stock exchanges has been continuously declining this year, with average trading value decreasing from approximately 35,000 billion VND/session in the first quarter to 24,000 billion VND in the second quarter and nearly 19,000 billion VND in the third quarter.
"The decline in trading volume indicates that individual investors' money has gradually withdrawn from the stock market," Mr. Quan said.
According to Tuoi Tre newspaper, deposit interest rates for 6-12 month terms are commonly around 9% per year. Lending interest rates have also increased, reaching 12-13% per year; for some real estate loans, after the preferential period, the interest rate can reach 15-16% per year.
Ms. Ha Vo Bich Van, a financial advisor at FIDT Investment Consulting and Asset Management Company, also noted that some clients are beginning to readjust their asset allocation strategies.
With simple calculations, at a deposit interest rate of 9% per year, 1 billion VND can yield approximately 90 million VND in interest after one year. Furthermore, depositors are not subject to daily price fluctuations like with stocks, gold, or real estate.
Therefore, when deposit interest rates rise to a sufficiently attractive level, VND deposits become a significant counterweight to risky assets in portfolio allocation.

The real estate market is facing double pressure.
Observations on numerous real estate forums show that the term "selling at a loss" is appearing more and more frequently. From apartments, land plots, townhouses to resort villas, every segment is seeing advertisements for sale and deep discounts.
The real estate market is also under pressure as interest rates rise, but the impact is dual, affecting both borrowers and those with available funds.

For those borrowing to buy real estate, rising interest rates directly increase financing costs. For example, with a loan of 3 billion VND, a mere 2 percentage point increase in interest rates could result in an additional interest expense of approximately 60 million VND per year.
What about gold?
Unlike bank deposits, gold does not generate a recurring cash flow. Gold holders only profit when the price increases significantly enough, and they must also account for the difference between the buying and selling prices.
Grandma Ha Vo Bich Van FIDT, a financial advisor, noted that gold should not be viewed simply as "rising inflation means rising gold."
Gold prices are also influenced by real interest rates, the US dollar, expectations of global monetary policy, economic prospects, and safe-haven demand.
This means that high deposit interest rates are not enough to conclude that gold will fall in price or become less attractive than deposits.
For investors faced with the choice of allocating new funds, the calculation is different: when deposits yield higher returns than before, gold must have a sufficiently attractive prospect of price appreciation for investors to accept giving up the relatively certain interest from the bank.
For those with readily available cash, the issue lies in opportunity cost. While depositing money in a bank can yield significant interest without the risk of asset price fluctuations, investors will consider more carefully before investing a large sum in real estate, a channel that typically has low liquidity and incurs additional transaction and ownership costs.
A representative from SGI Capital stated that many home loans, after enjoying low interest rates for the past 1-2 years, have recently seen a sharp increase, rising to 13-16% per year.
Many people who borrowed money from banks for the first time to buy a house or invest in real estate in the last 4-5 years believed that interest rates would remain low for a long time and house prices would never fall. Therefore, they prepared very little financial contingency for the current scenario, where loan interest rates have doubled after the grace period ends, while house prices have fallen rapidly with liquidity plummeting.
According to SGI Capital, the pressure to repay principal and interest on loans is increasing rapidly and becoming overwhelming, exceeding the income of many households. Many will have to find ways to sell off assets to reduce debt and cover living expenses.
"The capital allocated to stock market investments will also have an impact on the overall movement of the entire economy," concluded an expert from SGI Capital.
With investment properties, the comparison isn't simply about how much the house price increases compared to savings interest rates. The effectiveness of the investment also depends on rental income, the rate of increase or decrease in property value, cost of capital, taxes and fees, and liquidity.
Therefore, when deposit interest rates rise, real estate doesn't necessarily become a less attractive investment channel, but buyers' "expectations" will be higher: the investment must be attractive enough to compensate for the benefits they forgo by not depositing money in the bank.
Cash flow is not solely dependent on interest rates.
So what could bring money back into the stock market?
According to Mr. Quan Vu, Deputy Head of the Securities Research Department at Vietcap, interest rate trends remain one of the key variables determining the relative attractiveness of deposits versus stocks.
However, the flow of money in the market does not depend solely on interest rates.
The business performance of listed companies is also a noteworthy factor. In addition, geopolitical developments, such as the US- Iran and Russia-Ukraine conflicts; trade and tariff negotiations between the US and its partners, including Vietnam; and changes in domestic fiscal and monetary policies are also important considerations.
Another factor is the ongoing improvement of institutional and trading infrastructure, thereby meeting the criteria of international rating agencies and aiming for higher ratings within FTSE Russell, as well as the goal of being considered for an upgrade by MSCI.

"We maintain a fairly positive view on the profit growth of listed companies in the coming quarters and believe this will be one of the key factors supporting the return of capital to the market," Mr. Vu said.

articles.title: Anchors, Not Approvals: Vietnamese Lessons for India’s Foreign Investment Problem - Countercurrents.org
articles.summary: Anchors, Not Approvals: Vietnamese Lessons for India’s Foreign Investment Problem  Countercurrents.org
articles.full_text:
India’s foreign investment crisis is easy to miss behind the headline figures. Gross FDI reached a record $94.5 billion in FY2025-26, yet net FDI was only $7.7 billion after repatriation and outward investment. India is attracting substantial capital without retaining much of it as productive investment, while weak private CapEx makes it harder to turn foreign capital into a sustained expansion of productive capacity.
Vietnam is an important point of comparison: by the World Bank’s measure, its net FDI inflows were about 4.2 per cent of GDP in 2024, against roughly 0.7 per cent for India, and it reached that position from almost no capital or industrial capability. Its achievement lay in building the conditions under which foreign investment became long-term, reinvested and embedded in domestic capability.
From isolation to the centre of Asian manufacturing
Few developing countries have transformed their economic position as dramatically as Vietnam. When the Communist Party launched Đổi Mới in 1986, the country was emerging from decades of civil war, American war crimes and wars against Maoist China and Pol Pot’s Cambodia into an economic system characterised by central planning, collectivisation, shortages and severe macroeconomic instability. Inflation had exceeded 700 per cent, agricultural incentives had been badly distorted and a historically significant rice producer had become a net rice importer. Vietnam was also isolated by Washington’s hostility, tied to the fast-crumbling Soviet bloc and short of capital, industry and technology.
Barely four decades later, it is one of the most successful export-oriented manufacturing economies on earth. Real GDP growth averaged around 7 per cent between 1990 and 2010 and stayed above 6 per cent for most of the following decade, before dipping during Covid and rebounding to 8.5 per cent in 2022, 7.1 per cent in 2024 and 8.02 per cent in 2025. GDP per capita has risen from roughly $100 in the late 1980s to about $5,115 in 2026, while merchandise exports, only a few billion dollars at the start of the reform period, reached approximately $475 billion in 2025. Electronics, electrical machinery, computers, phones, machinery, garments and footwear now dominate its export basket. Crucially, foreign-invested firms generated 77.3 per cent of Vietnam’s goods exports in 2025.
The most striking feature is that Vietnam did not first build a sophisticated industrial base and then expose it to the world, but opened up precisely because it lacked the capital and capabilities to industrialise alone. The 1987 Law on Foreign Investment, enacted barely a year after Đổi Mới, recognised that foreign capital could provide more than finance: Vietnam also needed engineers, production technology, management systems, international customers, quality standards, logistics and access to global supply chains. Alongside this, the state liberalised agriculture, reformed land use, developed industrial zones, restructured banking and built a legal framework for private enterprise.
These reforms were complemented by extensive international integration. Vietnam joined ASEAN, normalised relations with the United States in 1995, concluded the US Bilateral Trade Agreement in 2000 and joined the WTO in 2007, before entering the CPTPP, EVFTA and RCEP. Multinationals consequently came to treat Vietnam as a manufacturing platform connected to some of the world’s largest economies. The reforms reinforced one another, as investment, trade integration, infrastructure and institutional change raised the returns to each.
Anchor investments and the architecture of credibility
Vietnam’s approach was far more interesting than the familiar story of a low-wage country competing mainly with tax breaks. The state understood that it lacked industrial capabilities and supporting industries as well as capital. Its approach in practice resembled an anchor investment strategy, in which large multinational projects were valued for their capacity to attract suppliers, build skills and infrastructure, and make further investment more viable.
Intel committed $1 billion in 2006 to an assembly and testing facility in Ho Chi Minh City’s High-Tech Park, later expanding it to $1.5 billion. Two years later, Samsung entered with a mobile-phone plant in Bac Ninh worth around $670 million. That initial investment was modest, but Samsung kept expanding and had raised its cumulative investment to roughly $19 billion by 2022 and about $24 billion by the end of 2025.
Such an investment creates demand for suppliers, logistics, engineering and specialised labour. Rather than simply maximising FDI approvals, Vietnam used these projects to catalyse a dense ecosystem. Other manufacturers followed, making Vietnam an integrated node in their production systems rather than merely an assembly site.
The same logic explains Vietnam’s extensive use of bilateral investment agreements, with UNCTAD listing 67 BITs and 33 treaties containing investment provisions. A multinational building factories, supplier networks and a trained workforce makes highly specific investments that cannot easily be moved, creating a classic hold-up problem. Investment treaties can strengthen the credibility of government commitments not to exploit this vulnerability, while trade agreements and domestic investment laws constrain arbitrary policy reversal. India’s retroactive taxation shows how quickly confidence can erode when such constraints are weak.
Vietnam thus used international commitments as part of a broader credibility architecture. Combined with actual investment, expanding export markets, industrial infrastructure and increasingly predictable institutions, they reshape investors’ expectations about the returns to long-term commitment.
Reform as a process of experiment and feedback
Vietnam’s transformation was shaped by experimentation and feedback rather than a perfectly designed blueprint. Provincial authorities gave farmers and producers greater autonomy before national policy had caught up, and stronger incentives produced dramatic increases in agricultural output. By 1989 Vietnam was exporting around 1.4 million tonnes of rice in 1989, a year after Resolution 10 gave farmers long-term land-use rights: the country was a net importer only a few years earlier. Yet while foreign companies enjoyed a liberal legal environment, Vietnamese entrepreneurs still faced permissions and capital requirements, and pressure from businesses and reform-minded officials made this contradiction hard to sustain, culminating in the 1999 Enterprise Law, implemented in 2000, which established a much stronger presumption that citizens could establish businesses unless explicitly prohibited.
Each reform revealed new constraints that shaped the next, raising the returns to earlier reforms and creating powerful path dependence. Once multinationals established production networks, suppliers had incentives to locate nearby, workers to acquire relevant skills, and later investors could enter an existing ecosystem rather than an unknown market. Samsung’s presence was therefore not a lucky investment but evidence of institutional transformation: Vietnam had spent two decades building the conditions under which Samsung would invest billions and reinvest billions more.
What India can learn from Hanoi
India’s much larger domestic market, federal structure and stronger corporate base make direct imitation impossible, but the underlying logic transfers. The objective should be an institutional architecture in which productive foreign investment becomes long-term, reinvested and embedded in domestic capabilities, which is what the gap between $94.5 billion gross and $7.7 billion net suggests is missing. Weak private CapEx compounds the difficulty, because anchors only generate supplier ecosystems when domestic firms invest alongside them.
Vietnam’s own figures are instructive here. Disbursed FDI, meaning capital actually spent on projects, reached a record $27.6 billion in 2025, with around 83 per cent going into manufacturing. The measures are not identical to India’s, but the contrast is clear: Vietnam’s headline is smaller than India’s gross figure and comes from an economy a fraction of the size, yet it is overwhelmingly capital committed to production.
India already has a candidate in Micron’s semiconductor assembly and test facility at Sanand, Gujarat, which opened in February 2026 with combined investment of about $2.75 billion by the company and government partners. Like Intel’s Ho Chi Minh City plant, it assembles and tests wafers made elsewhere. Whether Sanand becomes a true anchor depends on substrate makers, materials firms and equipment providers co-locating with it. Public support is substantial, with the Centre covering half the project cost and Gujarat another fifth. The test is whether that subsidy creates a lasting supplier base.
Apple offers a second test, benchmarked against Samsung in Vietnam. On speed India compares well, with more than $50 billion of iPhone exports in the four years to December 2025 and its supplier base rising from 14 firms in 2023 to over 40, ahead of Vietnam’s 35-plus. On depth, however, domestic value addition remains 18 to 23 per cent, below the government’s 35 to 40 per cent target. Vietnam still relies heavily on imported inputs, with foreign value-added accounting for about 48 per cent of exports in 2020. But Samsung’s network had expanded to 306 Vietnamese companies by early 2025, and its roughly $55 billion in exports accounted for 16 per cent of national exports in 2023. The point is not complete domestic self-sufficiency, but the creation of a growing domestic ecosystem around foreign investment.
The same approach should extend to pharmaceuticals, machinery and batteries, with trade agreements ensuring Indian production reaches global markets. Despite much fallacious thinking to this effect, India’s domestic market cannot substitute for integration

articles.full_text:
According to the ADB, shifting the growth model is no longer an option, but a requirement to help Vietnam overcome the middle-income trap and move towards the goal of becoming a high-income country by 2045.
Loading and unloading export goods at Hai Phong International Container Port. (Photo: Vu Sinh/VNA)
With traditional drivers reaching their limits, transforming the growth model is no longer an option, but a necessity of the times. The Asian Development Bank (ADB) assesses that Vietnam has made significant progress in this growth model transition.
However, to maintain long-term sustainable development momentum, the ADB believes that Vietnam's transformation is not yet complete and many major challenges remain to be addressed.
Great strides
In an interview with a VNA reporter, Mr. Bui Minh Giap, Chief Economist of the ADB in Vietnam, stated that thanks to the persistent implementation of an open-door policy, attracting foreign direct investment (FDI), focusing on infrastructure investment, and leveraging its competitive workforce, Vietnam has made significant progress from a low-income economy to an important manufacturing and export hub in the region.
Commenting on this milestone, Mr. Bui Minh Giap emphasized that Vietnam has risen to become an upper-middle-income country sooner than the target set for 2030.
Previously, according to the World Bank Group's annual country classification, Vietnam's gross national income (GNI) per capita increased from US$4,490 in 2024 to US$4,970 in 2025.
This income level officially exceeds the $4,636 threshold – the criterion for being classified as upper-middle income according to the organization's new classification. This progress marks a historic milestone after 17 years of Vietnam consistently being in the lower-middle income group (since 2009).
Commenting on Vietnam's growth momentum, at the press conference announcing the September Asian Development Outlook (ADO) report, Shantanu Chakraborty, ADB Country Director for Vietnam, praised Vietnam's positive economic performance in the first half of the year despite the volatile global context.
Vietnam's Gross Domestic Product (GDP) grew impressively by 8.2% in the first half of 2026, significantly higher than the 7.5% growth rate of the same period last year.
Mr. Shantanu Chakraborty noted that this growth has been evenly distributed across many sectors, with the continuous expansion of the processing and manufacturing industry, a thriving domestic consumption, stable foreign direct investment (FDI) flows, and timely support policies.
Sharing this view, Mr. Bui Minh Giap emphasized that a noteworthy aspect of Vietnam's economy in recent times is that growth has not come from a single sector but has encompassed many industries: industry, construction, services, agriculture , consumption, investment, and trade.
In particular, he identified two very important drivers for the Vietnamese economy: investment and production. Foreign direct investment (FDI) is a bright spot, with registered and disbursed capital increasing in the first 6, 7, and 8 months of the year, showing that Vietnam continues to be an important destination in the regional production chain.
You may also like
In terms of manufacturing, the Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) for the manufacturing sector has remained above 50 points for the past 14 months, indicating continued expansion in the manufacturing sector, thereby supporting other sectors of the economy.
Given the better-than-expected signals, the September ADO report continues to forecast Vietnam as one of the fastest-growing economies in the developing Asia-Pacific region in 2026, with the strongest upward revision in the region.
The Asian Development Bank (ADB) has raised its forecast for Vietnam's economic growth in 2026 to 7.8%, a significant increase from the 7.2% figure given in its July report. The growth rate for 2027 is projected to slightly decrease to 7.6%, still higher than the 7.0% forecast given by the ADB in July.
Internal bottlenecks
Despite many positive developments, the ADB notes that Vietnam's growth model transformation is not yet complete. The economy remains heavily reliant on capital accumulation, bank credit, cheap labor, FDI, and imported raw materials.
According to the ADB, the first challenge lies in the excessive reliance on bank credit. By the end of 2025, total outstanding bank credit will be equivalent to 145% of GDP, while the corporate bond market remains thin, accounting for only about 10% of GDP.
Due to credit growth outpacing deposit growth, the loan-to-deposit ratio in many banks has approached or exceeded the regulated ceiling.
Thin capital buffers combined with prolonged maturity mismatches narrow the room for rapid credit expansion, especially long-term financing for large infrastructure projects. Therefore, continued reliance on bank financing could increase risks to the financial system, thereby hindering investment-driven growth.
In addition, Chief Economist Bui Minh Giap also noted the phenomenon of trade deficit when imports increase faster than exports.
Between January and July 2026, exports increased by 21.7% thanks to key items such as electronics and manufactured goods. However, imports surged by 34.8%, causing the merchandise trade deficit to widen to $20.5 billion.
Analyzing further, Mr. Bui Minh Giap argued that the trade deficit is not entirely a bad sign because it reflects expanding production activities, with businesses increasing imports of machinery, equipment, raw materials, and components to meet production needs.
However, he emphasized that the downside of this phenomenon is that it shows the reality that the domestic economy is still heavily dependent on imported inputs.
Another strategic challenge raised by ADB Country Director Shantanu Chakraborty is to increase the role of the domestic private sector.
According to the ADB report, between January and July this year, as many as 155,300 businesses withdrew from the market, although 187,200 businesses were newly established or resumed operations. The large number of businesses withdrawing from the market reflects the persistent pressure and difficulties that the private sector is facing.
You may also like
The ADB representative emphasized that the shift towards increasing the role of the domestic private sector does not mean downplaying the role of FDI. He affirmed that FDI remains crucial for growth, exports, technology, and employment.
The core issue is that Vietnam needs to enhance the capacity of its domestic private sector to better absorb the benefits of FDI and participate more deeply in value chains, especially since small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) account for up to 95% of the total number of businesses.
Alongside enhancing the capacity of domestic businesses, Mr. Bui Minh Giap believes that the key reform priority is shifting from a mindset of "attracting FDI projects" to "building a strong investment ecosystem around FDI areas".
According to him, investment screening and incentives should focus more on domestic added value, technology transfer, research and development (R&D) activities, domestic supply rate, labor skills enhancement, environmental protection efficiency, and the level of linkage with Vietnamese businesses.
Only in this way can high-quality FDI become a more powerful driving force for the growth of Vietnamese businesses and enhance national competitiveness in the long term.
The ADB Country Director for Vietnam emphasized that behind the impressive growth figures achieved, the key issue now lies in how Vietnam can maintain high growth momentum while improving the quality of growth.
To achieve this, shifting the growth model is no longer an option, but a requirement to help Vietnam overcome the middle-income trap and move towards the goal of becoming a high-income country by 2045.

Alongside strengthening domestic enterprises, Giap said a key reform priority is to shift from the mindset of “attracting FDI projects” to “building a strong investment ecosystem around the FDI sector”. 
Investment screening and incentives should place greater emphasis on domestic value added, technology transfer, research and development (R&D), local sourcing, workforce skills, environmental performance and linkages with Vietnamese businesses, he said. This would enable high-quality FDI to become a stronger driver of domestic business growth and improve national competitiveness over the long term. 
Chakraborty stressed that behind the impressive growth figures achieved so far, the key challenge now is how Vietnam can maintain high growth while improving its quality. 
To achieve this, transforming the growth model is no longer an option but a necessity if Vietnam is to avoid the middle-income trap and pursue its goal of becoming a high-income country by 2045, he said./.

Hanoi (VNA) – In September, major international media outlets and financial institutions offered positive assessments of Vietnam’s economic outlook, describing the country as a growth bright spot in Southeast Asia while highlighting notable developments in its financial market and fresh growth momentum from technological transformation. 
Solid growth foundation 
Reuters, Bloomberg and the World Bank (WB) continued to highlight Vietnam’s strong economic performance in the region. According to WB data, the country’s GDP surged from 16.24 billion USD in 1994 to 514.7 billion USD. 
Notably, measured by purchasing power parity, the Vietnamese economy has surpassed 1 trillion USD, providing a solid foundation for its goal of becoming a developed nation by 2045. 
A report jointly released by US global management consulting firm Bain & Company, Singaporean financial services group DBS and Singapore-based strategic consultancy Vriens & Partners said Vietnam remained a leading growth market in Southeast Asia, with baseline growth projected at 6.2%. 
Growth has been driven by its increasingly important role in global supply chains, as the country has become a key manufacturing link for multinational corporations such as Samsung, Intel and Foxconn. Foreign-invested enterprises currently account for around 70% of Vietnam’s total export turnover. 
A notable milestone in September was the official inclusion of the Vietnamese stock market among secondary emerging markets by UK index provider FTSE Russell. 
According to FTSE Russell, the move could help Vietnam attract around 6 billion USD in foreign capital. US asset manager Vanguard also announced plans to increase its investment in Vietnam to 2.5 billion USD, reflecting growing international investor interest in the Vietnamese market. 
Embracing technology wave 
Domestic manufacturing has also shown a strong recovery. According to the S&P Global Manufacturing Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI), the PMI of Vietnam's manufacturing sector stood at 53.3 in August 2026, marking the 14th consecutive month above the 50-point threshold and the strongest improvement since the beginning of the year. 
Commenting on the recovery, S&P Global noted that a key strength of Vietnam’s manufacturing sector is businesses’ ability to optimise operational efficiency. Despite global geopolitical uncertainties, companies have proactively cut costs and reduced excess labour to focus on boosting core output. This approach helped production expand at its fastest pace in more than two years. 
Meanwhile, the rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) and automation is reshaping Vietnam’s labour market. A survey by Japan’s Reeracoen Group and Rakuten Insight showed that among six surveyed ASEAN markets, Vietnam recorded the highest proportion of businesses reporting improved revenue, at 46%, as well as the highest rate of companies expanding recruitment, at 16%. Business confidence also remained relatively positive, with 59% of executives optimistic about their business prospects. 
According to Malaysia-based HR Asia, Vietnam is the only Southeast Asian market where AI and automation rank as the leading factor prompting workers to change careers, cited by 39% of respondents. 
The trend highlights the increasingly visible impact of technology on career choices in Vietnam and underscores the need for workers to adapt and upgrade their skills as the labour market undergoes rapid transformation./.
In line with the Politburo's Resolution No. 10-NQ/TW on boosting the foreign-invested economic sector, the northern port city of Hai Phong is stepping up economic, trade, and investment connections with Chinese partners, creating new growth opportunities and enhancing foreign direct investment (FDI).
Toyota Vietnam sold 7,114 vehicles in September, up 45% month-on-month, while hybrid sales doubled year-on-year in the first nine months of 2026, showing growing demand for hybrid vehicles as Vietnam’s auto market moves towards greater fuel efficiency and lower emissions.
Vietnam recorded nearly 149,700 newly established enterprises in the first nine months of 2026, up 3.2% year-on-year, with total registered capital rising 32.7% to over 1.88 quadrillion VND (71.6 billion USD).

Vietnam's total export and import turnover reached 117.69 billion USD in September, up 7.3% from the previous month and 42.4% year-on-year. Notably, the goods trade balance returned to a surplus of 1.27 billion USD after nine consecutive months of deficit.
Prime Minister Le Minh Hung on October 3 called on ministries, sectors and localities to more effectively tap available growth potential, remove bottlenecks and maximise growth drivers in the final months of 2026, with the aim of achieving the year’s socio-economic development targets and creating momentum for 2027.

articles.summary: Singapore studies fusion as potential clean-energy pathway  sbr.com.sg

Gov’t studying fusion as potential clean-energy pathway
The METI places greater emphasis on energy security, economic growth and climate resilience.
Singapore is studying nuclear fusion as a potential low-carbon energy pathway as the new Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry (METI) places greater emphasis on energy security, economic growth and climate resilience.
The Ministry of Trade and Industry formally became METI on 1 October, reflecting the growing importance of energy to Singapore’s economic competitiveness and long-term resilience.
Speaking at FusionX 2026, Minister for Energy, Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) Tan See Leng said energy was an essential resource requiring long-term planning.
He said global developments had strengthened the need for Singapore to study emerging energy technologies and leave no potential pathway unexplored.
Fusion energy is one option the country is monitoring closely, although commercially operating fusion power plants could still be years away. Singapore has not decided whether to deploy any form of nuclear energy.
Fusion generates energy by combining atomic nuclei under extreme heat and pressure, unlike nuclear fission, which splits atoms.
The technology could produce lower levels of radioactive waste and has a limited risk of runaway reactions, but maintaining stable fusion conditions and achieving a net-positive energy return remain major technical challenges.
Singapore’s exploration of fusion forms part of its wider effort to diversify its energy sources and achieve net-zero emissions by 2050.
The country has increased its solar deployment target to 3 gigawatt-peak by 2030 after reaching its previous 2 GWp target ahead of schedule. It is also pursuing regional low-carbon electricity imports and studying the possible deployment of nuclear fission.
Singapore will participate in the International Atomic Energy Agency’s Integrated Nuclear Infrastructure Review in 2027 to assess its readiness to make an informed decision on nuclear fission.
Even without constructing a fusion reactor, Singapore could participate in the industry through its expertise in precision engineering, advanced manufacturing, plasma diagnostics and deep technology.
A*STAR has worked with US-based Realta Fusion since 2025 to develop a diagnostic tool that measures plasma velocities, helping researchers understand and control conditions within fusion systems.
The agency and Realta Fusion are exploring further collaboration in advanced plasma diagnostics and deployment.
SGInnovate and consulting firm Helixos have identified materials and coatings, plasma-facing components, diagnostics, software and control systems as potential areas for Singapore to enter the global fusion value chain.

articles.summary: Rubio says ‘foreign actor’ involved in alleged terror plot targeting British base used by US  Yahoo News SingaporeWhat we know and don't know about how Iran uses asymmetric warfare, Asia News  AsiaOneMan arrested in Fairford air base investigation released on bail  straitstimes.comUK-Iranian dual national arrested over RAF Fairford released on bail  BBCUK police arrest dual UK-Iranian man in Fairford air base investigation  CNA
articles.full_text:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said "the hands of a foreign actor" were involved in the suspected terror plot targeting a UK airbase used by the US military, revealing more about the investigation than British authorities – who have faced criticism from President Donald Trump.
"What happened this weekend could have been, and was, a very serious threat," Rubio told Fox News Monday night, adding there was "a lot more news" to come.
"It's one that clearly involved the hands of a foreign actor, I won't get into great detail about that yet," he added.
Five men, who have not been identified, were arrested early Sunday close to the base at Fairford in western England, from where US B-1 bombers have been flying missions against Iran.
But the suspects, who police said are all British nationals aged between 23 and 25 from the London area, were released on bail on Monday.
unknown content item
-
On Tuesday, Laurence Taylor, a senior counter-terrorism police officer, confirmed that "no improvised explosive devices were found" in vehicles. "However, a quantity of petrol was recovered," he added.
Police are planning to close down investigative operations at Fairford by Wednesday, he added.
Still, the decision to bail the suspects prompted criticism from US President Donald Trump, who said "I wouldn't have done that."
Taylor acknowledged that this decision had sparked surprise in some quarters, saying "I'd like to reiterate that it was investigative decision, and one which is grounded in experience and careful consideration of policing powers."
Trump said the suspects "might be" connected to Iran. "I know the answer, I can be very specific, but I'd rather not say it," he told reporters in the Oval Office.
Rubio's comments that the case "clearly" involved a foreign actor were less equivocal, though he declined to provide details.
"I think it ties us to the reality here. We are dealing with elements in the world, and in the case of Iran for example, who have openly threatened to attack American interests globally," he said.
Iran has strongly denied any involvement in the incident.
Rubio noted that people were "disturbed" by the news the suspects had been released, but said British authorities have been "very cooperative and on top of it."
The release of the five suspects does not mean that the investigation is over, and all five will be subject to stringent conditions on their movements, British counter-terrorism police said Monday.
Multiple British media outlets reported via sources that no explosives were found in the back of vans the men were driving and that the group's swift release on bail might indicate less imminent danger than initially feared. Britain's anti-terror laws allow police to hold suspects for up to 14 days.
Residents return
The UK has yet to publicly confirm any foreign link. Downing Street said it did not have an immediate response to Trump's comments, and directed CNN to earlier statements made by police.
Taylor said in a press conference earlier Monday police were considering the incident from every possible angle, "including that this may be actively committed by proxies or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly working on behalf of a foreign state."
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham chaired a meeting of COBRA - a committee that handles national emergencies - later Monday.
Interior minister Shabana Mahmood said that, as of Monday afternoon local time, "the scene is now safe." A police cordon remains around three vehicles found at the scene.
About 85 households, who were evacuated from the area on Sunday, were told by police on Monday evening that they can return to their homes.
unknown content item
-
Aerial footage on Sunday showed a bomb disposal robot roaming between the vans in woods near the base. The rear doors of two of the vans were open and large black items could be seen scattered on the ground nearby.
CNN teams nearby later heard what sounded like two controlled detonations from the direction of the village where the vans were found.
Iran denies involvement
Iran earlier denied any involvement in the incident. Its embassy in London issued a statement Monday saying it "strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran to arrest of five suspects in the vicinity of RAF Fairford base."
The Iranian embassy has yet to comment on Trump's remarks.
In July, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps specifically noted Fairford's use by US bombers, warning the UK that "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces."
On Sunday, Trump called the arrests "fantastic," saying the US and the UK had the men under investigation for "a long time."
However, UK authorities have not commented on that assertion. It's unclear whether the five men were under surveillance before their arrival in the Fairford area in the early hours of Sunday.
In their public statements British police say they were alerted to the men's presence near the base by local resdidents.
"Hooded and masked"
Photographs of the men – shirtless with their hands tied behind their backs – appeared in UK media Sunday.
They were initially detained under laws on possession of explosives and were later additionally arrested "on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act," according to a statement by counter-terrorism police.
A local resident said she came across the men when returning home on Saturday night.
"Both the driveway and the road were blocked by three white vans," she said.
The resident, who wishes to remain anonymous, told CNN that the vans were parked in a "strange formation" about 100 meters from the base fence.
She believed there were "definitely" more than five men in the group and most had their faces covered. However, authorities have not indicated they are looking for other individuals and said Sunday the situation had been contained. CNN is reaching out to police on the discrepancy.
Some ran into the field and some towards the neighboring village, the resident said.
She called the emergency services at 1:40 a.m., according to phone records she showed CNN. Within ten or 15 minutes, armed police arrived.
"I think it was pure luck that I arrived in the village at a similar time to the vans," the resident, a farmer, added.
UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the resident had "a partial picture" of the situation, adding that the work of the police and the security services "takes place often unsung, unreported, for good reason," he said.
Tightened security
Local people told CNN that security around the base had been tightened in recent days, with roadblocks at the entrance. But roads and lanes in the immediate area were still open.
The woman who called the police and one other local resident said that during previous conflicts, such as that against Iraq in 2003, there had been heavy security around the base. But security since the Iran conflict began has been less evident, they said.
A US Air Force spokesperson at Fairford – where the 501st Combat Support Wing is based – told CNN on Sunday: "For operational security reasons we will not discuss specific force protection measures."
CNN's Molly English, Lauren Kent and Lex Harvey contributed to this report.

All local stock sectors are expected to record positive earnings-per-share growth in the next financial year
OVER the past five decades, Singapore’s stock market has developed alongside the country’s rise as a global business and financial centre, while The Business Times has helped investors follow the companies, industries and market developments behind that progress.
The paper’s golden jubilee comes at a time when Singapore equities are entering a new phase, supported by stronger economic growth, broader earnings momentum, rising investor participation and measures aimed at strengthening capital formation, liquidity and research coverage.
The timing is significant. Singapore’s 2026 gross domestic product growth forecast has been raised to 5 per cent from 3.5 per cent in June, reflecting stronger expectations for manufacturing, non-oil domestic exports, bank lending, and finance and insurance.
The improvement is also showing up in company earnings. All local stock sectors are currently expected to record positive earnings-per-share growth in the following financial year, with technology, financial services and industrials among the stronger performers, while around 25 listed companies returned to profit in the latest reporting season.
With the Straits Times Index’s (STI) discount to analysts’ weighted target prices now much narrower than the average since end-2021, the market’s next gains will depend less on valuation catch-up and more on earnings, cash flow, capital returns and execution.
The STI tells only part of the story. Investors ultimately commit capital to companies, assessing their earnings, cash flow, balance sheets and ability to create value over time.
As listed companies report results, raise fresh capital, expand operations, pursue acquisitions and return cash to shareholders, clear reporting helps investors separate short-term market moves from longer-term business performance.
That is where BT has remained relevant over the past five decades, following the companies behind the headlines and helping investors understand what is changing and why it matters.
One measure of a market’s relevance is whether companies continue to use it to support their growth. Since 2017, about S$90 billion has been raised through Singapore’s equity market, with secondary fundraisings accounting for about four-fifths of the total.
Most are undertaken with a specific purpose, whether to fund acquisitions, increase capacity, enter new markets or support new growth initiatives.
Investors are rarely focused on fundraising alone. They want to understand what management intends to do with the capital and whether those plans can deliver stronger business performance over time.
That places greater importance on investor engagement, company communication and guidance. A fundraising may be completed in a matter of days, but investors often spend months and years assessing how the proceeds are deployed and whether the expected benefits are realised.
As companies provide updates on strategy, execution and performance, investors are better able to judge whether management is delivering on the objectives presented at the time capital was raised.
As more market activity becomes linked to business expansion, acquisitions, capacity investment and corporate transformation, the value of clear reporting and analysis will only increase.
The steady flow of results, disclosures and corporate developments creates a greater need for investors to understand not just what has happened, but also why it matters.
For five decades, BT has helped investors follow the developments shaping Singapore’s listed companies and capital markets. That role remains just as relevant today as investors assess not only what companies have done, but what they intend to do next.
The market itself is also becoming easier to follow.
Research coverage has expanded significantly in recent years, bringing more listed companies into the news and into investor discussion.
More initiations are being published, and more investors are gaining access to detailed analysis on business performance, industry developments and company strategy.
This is particularly relevant for small and mid-cap companies.
Many operate in industries that have benefited from Singapore’s economic development and regional growth, yet often receive less attention than the market’s largest names.
Broader research coverage gives investors more opportunities to study these companies while helping management teams communicate how they are deploying capital, growing earnings and building shareholder value over time.
Together with company disclosures, results announcements and investor engagement, broader research coverage helps investors stay informed and better understand the companies they follow.
BT continues to report on, scrutinise and provide context around these developments.
The changing profile of Singapore’s stock market is also worth noting. Financials remain its largest sector, reflecting the Republic’s position as a regional financial centre and one of the world’s leading wealth management hubs.
The three local banks account for close to 60 per cent of the STI, just over 20 per cent of the FTSE Asean All-Share Index, and continue to provide investors with exposure to regional growth, wealth management and cross-border capital flows. Their scale and profitability reflect decades of economic development, regulatory strength and international connectivity.
As Singapore’s market evolves, investors are also gaining exposure to a broader range of structural themes, including:
- Digitalisation and artificial intelligence;
- Advanced manufacturing;
- Regionalisation;
- Energy transition; and
- The Republic’s continued growth as a financial, wealth management and capital-raising hub.
While the underlying drivers may differ, all five themes are reshaping industries, capital allocation decisions and investment opportunities across our market.
However, themes alone do not create shareholder returns. Investors still need to assess how individual companies convert opportunities into results. In recent years, this has become increasingly apparent through a wider range of corporate actions and strategic initiatives.
Capital formation, capital returns, growth and transformation, asset optimisation, financial optimisation, value unlock, market recognition and corporate restructuring have all contributed to how companies create shareholder value and how investors assess them.
Many of the developments taking place across our market today can be viewed through these lenses.
Whether a company is raising capital to fund expansion, pursuing acquisitions, optimising assets, accelerating earnings growth or returning excess capital to shareholders, investors are increasingly looking beyond simple earnings metrics to understand the broader drivers of value creation.
The first 50 years established BT as a trusted observer of Singapore’s corporate and market development. The next 50 years should provide no shortage of companies, decisions and market developments worth following.
The writer is market strategist at SGX Group

A highlight is the Vietnam-Japan Cultural Village, covering nearly 7,000 square meters, adding green space and offering a unique cultural experience. This project also symbolizes the friendship between Vietnam and Japan, and marks a significant milestone in the cooperation between Nam Long and its Japanese partners. | 
| With an urban area spanning hundreds of hectares, amenities need to be developed at the pace of community formation and sustained over time. The facilities at Waterpoint are geared towards serving residents within the community while simultaneously expanding the value of the Ben Luc area. This approach represents a shift from simply providing housing products to building a vibrant urban ecosystem with long-term operational capabilities across multiple phases. Waterpoint's recognition as one of the "Top 10 Most Livable Urban Development Projects in Vietnam" at the 2026 Vietnam National Real Estate Awards demonstrates a clearly emerging symbol of comfortable living, operating practically and developing sustainably over time. |

Combined with the riverside landscape, these elements contribute to a tranquil lifestyle, contrasting sharply with the vibrant atmosphere of urban areas near the city center. |

Through each project, the Vietnamese-Japanese imprint is present in the amenities in operation, the community gradually grows, and the places evoke a sense of belonging. |
